{"id": "31:25/q09", "question": "What do most of them fail to know?", "turns_on": "Whether ignorance concerns monotheism's implications, failure to practice known truth, useful knowledge itself, exclusive creation and provision, or resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "31:25/q09/p1", "position": "They fail to grasp the proof and the consequence of their confession: God alone deserves praise and worship, without partners.", "reasons": "Muqatil names God's oneness; al-Tabari says they misplace praise and gratitude; al-Wahidi says association after confession exposes ignorance; al-Baghawi, al-Kashshaf, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, al-Alusi, al-Tabatabai, Asad, and Islahi emphasize the unheeded entailment. Al-Tabrisi says they miss the proof; al-Qurtubi attributes this to failure to consider or reflect. Abu Hayyan connects it to their invalid claim; Ibn Kathir says the confession is proof they do not understand. Al-Alusi adds ignorance of why God is praised here."}, {"id": "31:25/q09/p2", "position": "They know God controls matters, but fail to act on that knowledge by abandoning shirk.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi says knowledge without practice counts as no knowledge and can be worse than ignorance; Bursevi says their failure to worship God alone belies their admission."}, {"id": "31:25/q09/p3", "position": "They have no useful knowledge of God at all.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi reasons that genuine knowledge of God would benefit them; al-Razi regards an unrestricted denial of knowledge as more emphatic."}, {"id": "31:25/q09/p4", "position": "They do not affirm God's exclusive creation and provision.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi calls this contradiction one that obliges acceptance of the Prophet's claim of absolute divine unity."}, {"id": "31:25/q09/p5", "position": "They do not know that they will be resurrected.", "reasons": "Yahya ibn Sallam gives resurrection as the unrecognized matter."}]}
{"id": "31:25/q10", "question": "Does لَا يَعْلَمُونَ leave its object unstated?", "turns_on": "Whether an object is supplied from 'Praise be to God' or the verb remains absolute.", "positions": [{"id": "31:25/q10/p1", "position": "Yes; it absolutely denies knowledge, without any specific object.", "reasons": "Al-Razi likens the construction to saying someone gives and withholds without naming an object; he prefers its emphatic unrestricted force."}, {"id": "31:25/q10/p2", "position": "No; its understood object is that all praise belongs to God.", "reasons": "Al-Razi reports this second grammatical analysis but prefers the absolute construction."}]}
{"id": "31:25/q11", "question": "How does لَا يَعْلَمُونَ relate to the parallel لَا يَعْقِلُونَ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:25/q11/p1", "position": "The two endings convey the same meaning with a stylistic variation.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur compares this surah's wording with al-ʿAnkabut 29:63."}]}
{"id": "31:25/q12", "question": "What follows from acknowledging God as creator?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:25/q12/p1", "position": "Creation entails God's exclusive lordship, governance, praise, and worship; created idols cannot share His divinity.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf and al-Nasafi say the confession binds them to thank and worship God alone. Al-Razi argues that all creation needs Him; al-Qurtubi asks why they worship another; Ibn Kathir says the partners are God's property. Al-Biqaʿi says the idols are artifacts, not co-creators. Al-Tabatabai says governance cannot be separated from creation: God gives and withholds and alone is hoped for and feared. Asad says ultimate causation requires surrender. Islahi says others have no role in creating or governing. Kuran Yolu excludes divinity, divine function, sanctity, and worship for any other being. Islahi adds that God is self-sufficient and sovereign, so no intercessor is needed to win His favour."}]}
{"id": "31:25/q13", "question": "Can acknowledgment of God coexist with shirk, and how?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:25/q13/p1", "position": "Yes; people may profess God as creator while worshipping, invoking, or relying on idols and intermediaries.", "reasons": "Al-Damghani uses such profession as a sense of faith and compares the People of the Book's partial acceptance of scripture alongside rejection of other parts and messengers. Al-Qushayri says confessors return to error; al-Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, and Kuran Yolu describe partners worshipped despite the confession. Ibn Kathir says those partners are God's own creation and property; Kuran Yolu says Arab idolaters sought refuge in intermediary gods."}]}
{"id": "31:25/q14", "question": "Which incidents show people fearing an idol's power?", "turns_on": "The reports involve different people and different feared consequences.", "positions": [{"id": "31:25/q14/p1", "position": "A woman associated with Dhu al-Nur al-Dawsi feared children from Dhu al-Shara.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi reports her question as evidence that idols were thought able to act."}, {"id": "31:25/q14/p2", "position": "Dammam ibn Thaʿlaba's people feared leprosy and vitiligo after he reviled their gods.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi reports their warning to him."}, {"id": "31:25/q14/p3", "position": "The custodian of al-ʿUwwa and Thaqif feared retaliation when cult objects were attacked.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi reports Thaqif's claim that the foundations would rage and al-Mughira ibn Shuʿba's excavation of them."}]}
{"id": "31:25/q15", "question": "What do idolaters do when afflicted?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:25/q15/p1", "position": "Especially at sea, they disavow their idols and attribute events to God.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi says this fits God's exclusive control."}]}
{"id": "31:25/q16", "question": "How does this verse connect with surrounding and parallel passages?", "turns_on": "The cited passages show different links: preceding criticism, later explanation, prophetic consolation, or parallel formulations.", "positions": [{"id": "31:25/q16/p1", "position": "It exposes the inconsistency of inherited polytheism condemned in 31:21.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says they imitate ancestors while admitting God created heaven and earth."}, {"id": "31:25/q16/p2", "position": "It consoles the Prophet after 31:23 by anticipating vindication of his truth and the deniers' falsehood.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says their admission already supports monotheism and their return will reveal the truth, even before resurrection."}, {"id": "31:25/q16/p3", "position": "Verses 31:26–29 explain why praise belongs to God alone.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu cites God's freedom to govern, incomprehensible knowledge, and effortless power to create, sustain, or end all things."}, {"id": "31:25/q16/p4", "position": "The same admission or argument appears in parallel passages.", "reasons": "The Study Quran cites 10:31, 23:84–85, 29:61, 29:63, 39:38, 43:9, and 43:87; al-Alusi directs readers to his discussion of 29:61; al-Biqaʿi contrasts this verse's concise answer with 43:9; Ibn Ashur compares the end with 29:63."}]}
{"id": "31:25/q17", "question": "What inward path and outcome does this confession call to mind?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:25/q17/p1", "position": "Trust, reliance, sincerity, turning from all else, tawhid, and obedience lead to Paradise and nearness; disbelief, shirk, display, and reputation seeking lead to fire and separation.", "reasons": "Bursevi gives the two paths; he quotes ʿAttar's couplet that worldly success helps at the end only with sincerity, otherwise the soul is lost."}]}
{"id": "31:26/q01", "question": "What does it mean that all in the heavens and earth belongs to God?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:26/q01/p1", "position": "Every being and thing, including idols and their worshippers, is God's creation, servant, and possession, subject to His sovereign disposal.", "reasons": "Muqātil calls creatures His servants within His dominion. Al-Ṭabarī explicitly includes idols and all things whether worshipped or not; Ibn ʿĀshūr includes idolaters and their idols. Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Ālūsī add unrestricted disposal and control. Al-Rāzī gives a rational proof: contingent created things depend ultimately on a necessary being, directly for Ahl al-Sunna or through an intermediary for others; he also compares ownership of all that emerges from owned land. Al-Biqāʿī and al-Qurṭubī ground ownership in creation; al-Biqāʿī invokes the disbelievers' admission that God created it. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says creation entails governance and that absolute independence entails exclusive ownership and disposal. Iṣlāḥī and Kuranyolu add that everything is subject to and dependent on Him; Kuranyolu stresses His unrestricted freedom in creation and governance. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the idolaters' contrary statements lack reality."}]}
{"id": "31:26/q02", "question": "Why is ما في and the preposition not repeated before earth?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:26/q02/p1", "position": "The preceding admission of God's creation already establishes that earth is included, so repeating the expression is unnecessary.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī points to the prior proof and admission of creation as sufficient for earth's inclusion."}]}
{"id": "31:26/q03", "question": "What does God's ownership imply about worship and supposed partners?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:26/q03/p1", "position": "Only God deserves worship and has lordship; His possessions, including idols, cannot be independent rivals or claim worship or gratitude.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and Bursevī infer exclusive worship from universal ownership. Al-Biqāʿī says the idolaters' admission of God's creation leaves no partner. Al-Ālūsī argues that a possession cannot be its owner's partner or claim its due. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says creation necessarily entails governance and disposal, establishing exclusive lordship and divinity, while no other can independently own or govern. Ibn ʿĀshūr says owning ido

{"id": "31:26/q04", "question": "What force do هو and the definite epithets add?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:26/q04/p1", "position": "They emphatically restrict unmatched self-sufficiency and praise to God and exclude supposed gods.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says the explicit divine name and emphatic هو answer the implied denial of self-sufficiency in associating partners and affirm the attributes without limit. Bursevī says هو confines self-sufficiency to God, citing 47:38 on God's riches and human need. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls هو a separating pronoun restricting both attributes, with a reference to 31:12. Samarrāʾī contrasts the definite الغني الحميد after ownership with bare غني حميد where possession is unmentioned: the former marks unmatched wealth and praise."}]}
{"id": "31:26/q05", "question": "How does the wording here compare with al-Ḥajj 22:64?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:26/q05/p1", "position": "This verse uses هو and definite epithets; 22:64 adds a lām before هو, giving further emphasis, though the cited excerpts leave its reason unanswered.", "reasons": "Both Samarrāʾī notes observe this contrast and explicitly pose, without answering, why the additional lām occurs in 22:64."}]}
{"id": "31:26/q06", "question": "What does al-Ghanī mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:26/q06/p1", "position": "God is absolutely self-sufficient, needing nothing from creation, including its worship or praise, while creatures need Him.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī glosses the word as the opposite of needy. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Bursevī say He needs nothing for existence or perfection; Bursevī extends this to before and after creation and to essence and attributes. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Kashshāf, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Ṭībī specify independence from worshippers' praise or worship; al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī and Iṣlāḥī contrast universal creaturely need. Al-Rāzī says God's ownership benefits Him in no way and unbelievers' lack of praise cannot diminish Him. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues that the source of creation and giver of every perfection must possess all that beings need, or He could not originate or give it; His independence entails ownership without a competing independent governor. Bursevī cites 47:38. Samarrāʾī says the form after the ownership clause marks unmatched wealth and praise. Study Quran refers readers to its note on 31:12 for these names without giving a further gloss here."}]}
{"id": "31:26/q07", "question": "What does al-Ḥamīd mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the name expresses worthiness for praise regardless of its occurrence, praise actually given, or the act of ascribing praiseworthy qualities.", "positions": [{"id": "31:26/q07/p1", "position": "God inherently deserves praise, whether anyone praises Him or not, for His perfections, beautiful acts, creation, and benefits.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī makes the term the opposite of blameworthy. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Bursevī locate praiseworthiness in God's essence and attributes; Bursevī says He praises Himself even if no one else does. Al-Ṭabarī cites blessings and 14:1; al-Qurṭubī His acts; Abū Ḥayyān creation and gifts; Ibn Kathīr creation, law and all affairs; al-Biqāʿī absolute benefaction. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī defines ḥamd as praise for chosen beauty: all worldly beauty is God's, so all praise returns to Him; independent beautiful governance by another would contradict His absolute praiseworthiness. Iṣlāḥī says every praiseworthy attribute is His, so gratitude belongs to Him alone. Al-Ālūsī reports this as one sense. Study Quran refers to its note on 31:12 without adding a gloss here."}, {"id": "31:26/q07/p2", "position": "God is actually praised by creation, by its speech or state, for His sovereignty and acts.", "reasons": "Muqātil says He is praised among creatures in His sovereignty; Yaḥyā says creatures praise Him and are charged to do so. Al-Ṭabarī links praise to His blessings; al-Qurṭubī to His acts; Ibn Kathīr to creation, law and all affairs. Al-Biqāʿī says every tongue praises Him and even blameful speech is praise insofar as God caused it. Al-Ālūsī reports actual praise by every creature through its state as an alternative to mere deservingness."}, {"id": "31:26/q07/p3", "position": "Al-Ḥamīd can denote one who describes Himself or His servants with praiseworthy qualities.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī adds that a human ḥamīd can likewise mean one who describes himself or others with praiseworthy qualities, or a grateful worshipper."}]}
{"id": "31:26/q08", "question": "How do God's self-sufficiency and praiseworthiness work together here?", "turns_on": "The notes give three rationales for joining independence and praise: praise cannot benefit God, His beneficence benefits creatures, or absolute wealth grounds absolute praiseworthiness.", "positions": [{"id": "31:26/q08/p1", "position": "God needs no praise, yet deserves it regardless of whether creatures give it.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī gives this as his second explanation: unbelievers' failure to praise cannot diminish God, while believers' praise is vindicated and completed. Al-Kashshāf, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Ṭībī likewise contrast independence from praise with inherent worthiness. Al-Ālūsī reports al-Ṭībī's additional point that ownership belittles idolaters and removes any need for their worship."}, {"id": "31:26/q08/p2", "position": "God gains nothing from owning creation, while His creation and beneficence meet human needs and merit praise.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī presents this as his first explanation. Al-Ālūsī says the second epithet signals beneficence and perfections while the first rules out owning things from need. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī connects God's giving every perfection with His independence and says all beauty returns praise to Him."}, {"id": "31:26/q08/p3", "position": "Because needy creatures praise whoever supplies their needs, only the absolutely self-sufficient can be absolutely praiseworthy.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī gives this as his third explanation of the pair."}]}
{"id": "31:26/q09", "question": "Why are creatures obliged to praise or worship God if He needs neither?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:26/q09/p1", "position": "The obligation benefits creatures themselves; their worship and praise supply no need in God.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā says God made creatures duty-bound to praise Him. Al-Qurṭubī explains that His commands are for their own benefit. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Ṭībī stress that God has no need of polytheists' or other creatures' worship and praise."}]}
{"id": "31:26/q10", "question": "How does this verse follow the preceding admission about creation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:26/q10/p1", "position": "God's universal ownership follows from the admitted creation of heaven and earth, exposing the idolaters' disbelief and claims to partners.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the ownership sentence a result and inclusive apposition to what precedes, comparing the reasoning at 31:16; he says the stated conclusion belittles their disbelief because they and their idols belong to God. Al-Biqāʿī says the disbelievers' own admission of His creation leaves no room for a partner and renders repetition about earth unnecessary. Al-Ṭībī, reported by al-Ālūsī, says the ownership statement belittles idolaters and shows that God needs neither them nor their worship or praise."}]}
{"id": "31:26/q11", "question": "How does the following verse relate to this ownership statement?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:26/q11/p1", "position": "It counters an inference that God's dominion is finite by presenting boundless wonders of His power and knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the preceding ownership statement could suggest a finite dominion, which the next verse corrects."}]}
{"id": "31:26/q12", "question": "What reading of the following verse is reported?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:26/q12/p1", "position": "Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb read al-baḥra in the accusative, coordinated with the syntactic position of mā, meaning 'and if the sea.'", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports the readers and gives coordination with the syntactic position of mā as the grammatical explanation."}]}
{"id": "31:26/q13", "question": "What spiritual practice or outcome is drawn from the verse?", "turns_on": "The notes offer different devotional applications: a broad path of sincerity and obedience, and persistence in a particular invocation.", "positions": [{"id": "31:26/q13/p1", "position": "Sincerity, reliance on God, tawḥīd, and obedience lead to Paradise and nearness; hypocrisy and shirk lead to loss and separation.", "reasons": "Bursevī commends entrusting oneself to God, turning from all else, sincerity and obedience, opposing them to disbelief, shirk, showing off and reputation-seeking, which lead to fire. He quotes ʿAṭṭār's couplet that worldly success helps in the end only with sincerity; otherwise the soul is lost."}, {"id": "31:26/q13/p2", "position": "Persistence in an invocation praising God's acts and beneficence brings immeasurable wealth.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports an Idrīsian invocation calling God praiseworthy in action and beneficent to creation; al-Suhrawardī gives the promised result for persistence in it."}]}

{"id": "31:27/q02", "question": "How does annamā function after law?", "turns_on": "Whether law licenses a nominal predicate and whether an existential predicate is supplied.", "positions": [{"id": "31:27/q02/p1", "position": "The anna clause has mā as noun and aqlām as nominal predicate.", "reasons": "Sībawayh says annamā can stand where anna can, unlike independent innamā; al-Mubarrad makes the clause a subject of implied existence, while others move an omitted predicate before or after. Al-Ṣaffār and poems support the construction."}, {"id": "31:27/q02/p2", "position": "A nominal predicate after law anna is valid and refutes a strict verbal requirement.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn cite common Arabic and poems; Ibn al-Ḥājib concurs."}, {"id": "31:27/q02/p3", "position": "A verbal predicate is required only with a derived predicate; aqlām is outside that rule.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī narrows al-Zamakhsharī's rule and excludes a wish construction at 33:20."}, {"id": "31:27/q02/p4", "position": "The noun after law is subject to an omitted existential verb.", "reasons": "Burhān reports the Kufan estimate 'if it were established that.'"}]}
{"id": "31:27/q03", "question": "What does min shajaratin specify?", "turns_on": "Whether specification attaches to mā or its locative pronoun.", "positions": [{"id": "31:27/q03/p1", "position": "It specifies mā or its locative pronoun and encompasses the whole class of earthly trees.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, al-Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī give these grammatical analyses; al-Ālūsī compares an indefinite in a conditional and Ibn ʿAbbās's date-and-locust analogy."}]}
{"id": "31:27/q04", "question": "Why is shajarah singular?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular distributes each tree or names the whole class.", "positions": [{"id": "31:27/q04/p1", "position": "It distributes the picture tree by tree until none is omitted.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Rāzī, Biqāʿī and Bursevī stress exhaustive individual treatment."}, {"id": "31:27/q04/p2", "position": "It denotes the class; each tree can yield many pens from its branches.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān cites indefinite singular parallels at 2:106 and 35:2; al-Ālūsī objects that a lone singular does not formally mean 'tree by tree' and one pen per tree would weaken the image; Ibn ʿĀshūr describes suitable branches."}]}
{"id": "31:27/q05", "question": "What is aqlām?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:27/q05/p1", "position": "Pens are cut and sharpened writing tools, potentially many from each tree.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī describes trimmed branches; Bursevī derives qalam from cutting and distinguishes kinds of cutting; Ibn ʿĀshūr describes a split reed. Al-Ālūsī calls aqlām formally a paucity plural because qilām is rare."}, {"id": "31:27/q05/p2", "position": "No parallel supply of pens is needed, because one pen writes many books.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī contrasts quickly consumed ink with a pen's long use; al-Biqāʿī infers omitted ink and more trees."}]}
{"id": "31:27/q06", "question": "Which sea is intended?", "turns_on": "Whether the article points to the known ocean, all seas, or fresh water.", "positions": [{"id": "31:27/q06/p1", "position": "The sea generically, including Earth's seas.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī make the first sea generic; al-Ṭībī takes its article as replacing Earth's possessive pronoun."}, {"id": "31:27/q06/p2", "position": "The great encircling ocean.", "reasons": "Bursevī describes its inlets, depth, islands, jinn cities and Iblīs's throne; al-Ālūsī prefers the known greatest sea."}, {"id": "31:27/q06/p3", "position": "Fresh water that grows trees for pens.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbaydah argues salt water cannot grow the pens; Majāz notes inland country may also be called a sea."}, {"id": "31:27/q06/p4", "position": "Bahr lexically denotes broad or abundant water and can have figurative uses.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī cites a broad-striding horse, a prophetic use for abundance, briny water poetry, bāḥir for a fool and baḥrah for a locality."}]}
{"id": "31:27/q07", "question": "How is al-baḥr read?", "turns_on": "Which transmitted case or wording is followed.", "positions": [{"id": "31:27/q07/p1", "position": "Accusative al-baḥra, attributed chiefly to Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid says Abū ʿAmr alone in his list; al-Nashr names two Basrans, while other accounts add Ibn Abī Isḥāq and ʿĪsā. Al-Ṭabarī accepts both cases."}, {"id": "31:27/q07/p2", "position": "Nominative al-baḥru, the majority reading.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid and al-Fārisī name the majority; Ibn ʿUmar reports prophetic nominative recitation. Al-Ṭabarī accepts both cases."}, {"id": "31:27/q07/p3", "position": "Indefinite nominative wa-baḥrun is read by Ibn Masʿūd and Ṭalḥah.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinnī supplies 'there is a sea'; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn allow a circumstantial wāw; al-Ālūsī prefers the stated verb as predicate."}, {"id": "31:27/q07/p4", "position": "Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad reads 'the sea is its ink' (madāduhu).", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyyah calls madād a verbal noun; al-Ṭabrisī rejects taking seawater merely as addition to other ink."}]}
{"id": "31:27/q08", "question": "How is the sea clause parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether it is circumstantial or coordinated within the law clause.", "positions": [{"id": "31:27/q08/p1", "position": "It is a new circumstantial nominal clause with al-baḥr as subject and yamudduhu as predicate.", "reasons": "Sībawayh estimates 'the sea is in this state'; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī prefer wāw al-ḥāl, with no linking pronoun required. {"id": "31:27/q10", "question": "What does yamudduhu mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb evokes ink supply or a general extension.", "positions": [{"id": "31:27/q10/p1", "position": "Seven seas continually replenish the first as ink replenishes an inkpot.", "reasons": "Al-Yazīdī compares adding water to a pot; al-Zamakhsharī, Nasafī and al-Ālūsī use an inkwell image; al-Ālūsī notes the imperfect form, and Ibn ʿĀshūr says ink is implicit."}, {"id": "31:27/q10/p2", "position": "Madda extends or adds gradually, while amadda denotes external assistance or supply.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī, Abū Zayd, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and al-Qurṭubī report distinctions, comparing rivers, wells, money and troops; Ibn Qutaybah connects this use to midād ink."}, {"id": "31:27/q10/p3", "position": "Madda and amadda can be synonymous dialect variants.", "reasons": "Groups reported by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and al-Qurṭubī, and Ibn al-Shaykh, see no material difference."}]}

{"id": "31:27/q19", "question": "Why use the plural kalimāt?", "turns_on": "Whether the small plural has force here.", "positions": [{"id": "31:27/q19/p1", "position": "Even a small number of God's words exceeds these supplies, all the more His total speech.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Biqāʿī, Bursevī and al-Ālūsī make the a fortiori claim; al-Samīn invokes Ḥassān's jufanāt."}, {"id": "31:27/q19/p2", "position": "A sound plural in a general construction need not mean a small number.", "reasons": "Al-Shaykh objects to the strict paucity reading; al-Samīn notes debate about whether the article marks generality."}]}
{"id": "31:27/q20", "question": "What does the image establish?", "turns_on": "Whether the comparison asserts a precise quantity or simply proves inexhaustibility.", "positions": [{"id": "31:27/q20/p1", "position": "Finite materials, pages, writers and lives cannot exhaust divine words, knowledge, decrees or signs.", "reasons": "Muqātil says all creation's pens would fail; al-Ḥasan says the writer dies; Ibn ʿAṭiyyah says adding more cannot establish a limit. {"id": "31:27/q21", "question": "What follows about divine speech?", "turns_on": "Whether kalimāt must denote eternal speech or can denote limitless referents.", "positions": [{"id": "31:27/q21/p1", "position": "God's speech is eternal and uncreated, so its meanings do not end.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī infers uncreatedness; al-Qurṭubī prefers eternal speech on contextual grounds; Bursevī infers Quranic pre-eternity; al-Rāzī distinguishes divine attribute from created letters."}, {"id": "31:27/q21/p2", "position": "Limitless knowledge and possibilities can be called words without treating them as eternal speech.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī confines some referents to future possibilities; Ibn ʿAṭiyyah observes this tends toward Muʿtazilī created-speech doctrine; al-Fārisī reports a wisdom-and-workmanship reading."}]}

{"id": "31:27/q30", "question": "How is the verse used in discussion of Quranic inimitability?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:27/q30/p1", "position": "Its composition and meanings exceed human learned rhetorical craft.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī contrasts teachable meter and badīʿ with consistent Quranic excellence; Burhān says varied retellings avoid tedium, with addition, omission and rearrangement; al-Rāghib says a short Quran holds uncountable meaning."}, {"id": "31:27/q30/p2", "position": "Its rhetoric calls for whole-Quran comparison of words, style and context.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ describes her lexical and comparative method, influence of her father and al-Khūlī, and the Arab eloquence miracle alongside Moses' and Jesus' signs."}, {"id": "31:27/q30/p3", "position": "The seven Ḥawāmīm emphasize revelation from the Mighty, Wise God.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes their consecutive revelation and canonical order, Ḥā Mīm openings, al-Shūrā's added letters and Arabic revelation formula."}]}
{"id": "31:27/q31", "question": "What ancillary comparisons do commentators make?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:27/q31/p1", "position": "Lexical and poetic comparisons illuminate broad Arabic usage.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinnī cites dialectal ṣād/sīn/zāy variation; al-Jurjānī discusses Abū Tammām's metaphor of poetic ideas and word craft; Burhān reports a variant of Jarīr's line."}, {"id": "31:27/q31/p2", "position": "Adjacent discussions address resurrection and cross-reference other sūras.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyyah reports a question about gradual growth and sudden resurrection; Ibn al-Jawzī cross-refers Hūd, al-ʿAnkabūt and al-Baqarah."}, {"id": "31:27/q31/p3", "position": "Innamā is a non-governing restrictive construction unlike dependent annamā.", "reasons": "Al-Khalīl and Sībawayh cite independent-clause examples; al-Jurjānī reports mā ... illā analyses and warns the two constructions are not interchangeable."}]}

{"id": "32:11/q08", "question": "What does the verse mean by death?", "turns_on": "Whether death is created directly or is a natural accident.", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q08/p1", "position": "Death is an existent quality created in opposition to life.", "reasons": "Bursevī states this account; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says God extinguishes animals' life and does the same in humans, while using angels for humans."}, {"id": "32:11/q08/p2", "position": "Death is a natural condition arising accidentally from an animal's constitution.", "reasons": "Bursevī rejects this account; Ālūsī regards reading the verse as its refutation as weak."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q09", "question": "Who is the Angel of Death?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular title names one appointed angel, a group, an angel for each person, or an inward universal soul.", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q09/p1", "position": "A particular angel, commonly called ʿAzrāʾīl, appointed to take souls.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Kalbī describe him with four wings and world-spanning reach; Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān gloss the name 'servant of God.' Ibn Kathīr finds a specific angel in the singular wording. Itqān transmits the name from Wahb through Abū al-Shaykh. Kuran Yolu notes its probable Hebrew origin and absence from the Qur'an and sound hadith; Jewish and Christian traditions also assign such work to an angel or angels. Study Quran gives the common identification."}, {"id": "32:11/q09/p2", "position": "The singular title can denote the class or leader of assisting angels.", "reasons": "Jishumī attributes many helpers to Qatāda, Muqātil, and al-Kalbī; Ṭabrisī calls the title collective in light of 6:61 and 4:97. Kuran Yolu compares the singular with plural angel verses and proposes leadership or helpers."}, {"id": "32:11/q09/p3", "position": "An angel is appointed over each person.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says this angel takes each person's soul and accompanies the deceased under God's sight until resurrection."}, {"id": "32:11/q09/p4", "position": "The universal human soul, receiving uncorrupted partial souls.", "reasons": "Qāshānī says souls retaining primordial nature return to it; angels of punishment separate those corrupted to the limit."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q10", "question": "What is the nature of an angel here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q10/p1", "position": "An angel is a subtle luminous body capable of taking different forms.", "reasons": "Bursevī gives the definition, and reports investigators distinguishing angels entrusted with administration, including the Angel of Death, from human rulers."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q11", "question": "What is the Angel of Death commissioned to do?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q11/p1", "position": "He takes souls at their appointed times and knows or records their lifespans.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās through Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Bayḍāwī, Nāṣafī, Bursevī, and Ālūsī state the charge. Rāzī says he neither neglects nor delays anyone at their term and that this is his sole task. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the unrestricted verse may imply more than the standard gloss of causing death and taking souls. Itqān's Ibn Sābiṭ assigns him souls among three angels whose records agree at resurrection; Gabriel handles scriptures, revelation, victory and destructive events, and Michael rain and plants."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q12", "question": "How do the Angel of Death and other angels take souls?", "turns_on": "Whether assistants participate, and if they do, whether they extract, seize or attend the souls.", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q12/p1", "position": "The Angel of Death takes souls with assisting angels of mercy and punishment.", "reasons": "Qatāda, al-Kalbī, Muqātil and later transmitters report helpers. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says their participation honors humans and heightens the disbelievers' punishment. Kuran Yolu cites 8:50 and 16:32–33 for plural angels and contrasts their gentle greetings to protected believers with blows and harsh words for the wicked (4:97, 7:37, 47:27). Study Quran cites 4:97, 8:50, 16:32."}, {"id": "32:11/q12/p2", "position": "He summons the souls, they answer, and he directs assistants to seize them.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī says angels grasp and draw spirits out while God creates death; Kashshāf, Nāṣafī and Burhān report the summons and command. Qurṭubī says he then hands souls to mercy or punishment angels."}, {"id": "32:11/q12/p3", "position": "Assistants draw souls from bodies; he receives them at the throat.", "reasons": "Baghawī's ladder report places him between heaven and earth. Ibn Kathīr calls this a hadith; Ālūsī says he takes the soul near its departure."}, {"id": "32:11/q12/p4", "position": "He takes souls by himself, without assistants.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports this as the alternative to taking them with assistants."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q13", "question": "How can the angel, other angels, and God each be said to take souls?", "turns_on": "How to reconcile 39:42's divine attribution with this verse and passages naming plural angels.", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q13/p1", "position": "God creates or ultimately causes death, while the angel and helpers carry out its taking.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī distinguishes God's creation from the angels' grasping and drawing; Jishumī prefers the angel's seizure or command of helpers. Ṭabrisī cites 39:42 and says none but God controls death. Qurṭubī invokes 39:42 and 67:2; angelic execution accounts for 6:61 and 8:50. Nāṣafī says God commands and creates acts. Burhān reports Baghawī's summons-and-extraction account. Ālūsī gives Ashʿarī acquisition or divine permission and will. Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes levels of causation, like pen, hand and person each writing. Study Quran reports Qurṭubī's reconciliation and cites 6:61–62 and 7:37; Elmalılı poses the attribution question but his excerpt ends before an answer."}, {"id": "32:11/q13/p2", "position": "God takes souls and orders angels to seize them.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this alternative but explicitly prefers the previous account, where the angel seizes the life-bearing spirit."}]}
{"id": "32:11/q14", "question": "Whose souls does the Angel of Death take?", "turns_on": "Whether the angel's charge covers animals and sea martyrs, or other angels or God take those souls.", "positions": [{"id": "32:11/q14/p1", "position": "Every creature's soul, including animals and even small insects.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā reports every land and sea creature; Ibn al-Jawzī connects this with the one-kind account of souls. Qurṭubī reports fleas and mosquitoes; Mālik answers yes about fleas and cites 39:42. The Anṣārī narration says he cannot take even a mosquito without God's command. Ālūsī calls this the majority position and names one angel with helpers."}, {"id": "32:11/q14/p2", "position": "Human souls go through the Angel of Death; God ends animals' lives without him.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports direct divine taking of animals and interprets it as extinguishing life, while humans receive angelic care as an honor; Qurṭubī repeats the report. Ibn al-Jawzī connects the view to a distinction between human and animal soul kinds."}, {"id": "32:11/q14/p3", "position": "Different angels take different creatures' souls.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās assigns separate angels to humans, jinn, devils, birds, wild animals, beasts, fish and ants; Ālūsī leaves the report's soundness to God."}, {"id": "32:11/q14/p4", "position": "God personally takes martyrs at sea as a special exception.", "reasons": "Abū Umāmah transmits the Prophet's exception; al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās also gives the honor as its reason."}]}
